query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, conformal ceria-based overlayer onto a near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst will enhance its low‐temperature oxidation activity, poison resistance (against H2O and NO), and lifetime durability without increasing platinum-group-metal use.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element alloy catalyst containing minimal platinum-group metals, which in its unmodified state exhibits adequate catalytic activity under clean conditions but suffers from rapid performance loss when exposed to typical automotive exhaust poisons and long-term thermal aging.
generation.intervention: Deposit a nanometer-scale (approximately 2–5 nm) ceria or ceria–zirconia mixed oxide overlayer on the catalyst surface via atomic layer deposition (ALD) to create a stable, oxygen-buffering, and sinter-resistant coating.
generation.conditions: Operate under simulated automotive exhaust conditions with a low-temperature window (around 100–150 °C) while exposing the catalyst to a gas mixture containing CO, hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO. Additionally, the catalyst should undergo accelerated aging protocols that include periodic high-temperature excursions (up to about 700 °C) to mimic mileage-related thermal degradation over a vehicle lifetime.
generation.structural_mediator: The conformal ceria-based overlayer that interfaces with the underlying multi-principal-element alloy, maintaining a high dispersion of active sites by reducing sintering and providing oxygen storage and redox capability at the catalyst surface.
generation.mechanism: The ceria-based coating facilitates rapid oxygen exchange at low temperatures through its oxygen storage-release capability, protecting the active sites from poisoning (by H2O and NO) and hindering nanoparticle agglomeration during thermal excursions. This enhances the catalytic oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons and preserves activity over long-term operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified catalyst, the coated catalyst is expected to show improved low-temperature oxidation activity, increased resistance to poisoning by exhaust constituents, and greater retention of catalytic activity after extended high-temperature aging cycles.
generation.baseline: The unmodified near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy catalyst which, while initially active, exhibits performance degradation under low-temperature, poisoning, and long-term aging conditions.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are expected under exhaust conditions typical of automotive operation (100–150 °C with relevant exhaust gas mixtures and accelerated aging cycles). The performance under conditions significantly outside these ranges (e.g., substantially higher gas temperatures or drastically altered gas compositions) remains untested.
generation.uncertainty: While the general redox and sintering-inhibition effects of ceria-based coatings are well established, the quantitative enhancement in low-temperature oxidation activity and long-term durability on a complex multi-principal-element alloy remains to be verified experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of catalysts: one set of the baseline near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy and another set with an ALD-deposited ~2–5 nm ceria-based overlayer. Subject both to simulated automotive exhaust conditions (including a gas mixture containing CO, hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO at 100–150 °C) and accelerated aging cycles with intermittent exposures to 700 °C to simulate mileage-related thermal degradation. Assess catalytic performance before and after aging.
measurements: Low-temperature catalytic conversion rates for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
Time-resolved catalytic activity under continuous exposure to the exhaust gas mixture.
Characterization of the catalyst surface (e.g., TEM, XRD, XPS) pre- and post-aging to observe sintering and chemical state changes.
Comparison of poisoning resistance by monitoring activity in the presence of H2O and NO.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ceria-coated catalyst does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in low-temperature catalytic activity, poisoning resistance, or retention of catalytic performance after accelerated aging compared to the unmodified catalyst, then the hypothesis will be falsified.
